name: NeuroSurge
model_scope: Separate model under development; no trained decoder is supplied or validated by this game.
signal_origin: simulated, unitless brain and muscle activity values
source_lineage: Body update (R558), fifteenth upload, built from the 10 November interaction update: a camera at your eyes with a 108-degree view; a body that (since 17 November) lies back as on a declined sofa, hips straight, back rounded and head upright, with every limb forward and a slight bend in a stretched elbow or knee; the mirror body as a literal reflection on the same ground; 54 motor areas, one colour each, shared by the brain area and its muscles on both bodies, with a neon flash and one line from a lit area to the body part it moves; movements held until the opposite area or Reset body; Space as the one hand key (hold or tap to take hold of the brain, the mirror body or a limb, tap twice to turn all four limbs at their far ends: the forearms and the ankles lead, the upper arms and thighs follow by a few degrees); reach keys that light only the shoulder and elbow parts of the strip and their muscles; an information card that names the strip part, the movement and the muscles, read with the R key; the glass brain in the upper part of the view with the mirror body below it, and a motor strip about 42 % of the view wide at 1920 by 1080; a numbered list of each motor area’s movements on the information card, done with the number keys 1 to 9, with “already there” on a movement that would not move the body; the left and right arrow keys stepping the look one motor area along the strip; an information card that takes an area when the look rests on it; a “Looking at” line that names the area and then its movement, and a card line that names the strip part and the half of the brain; a “Try this” guide that starts with area, number key, another body part and watching the body; knees that bend all the way and a hip area that swings the thigh down and back as well as up, out and in; a held trunk movement that bends the trunk under the head and keeps the view; a line at the bottom left after a head movement that says how to bring the head back; a mark on a movement whose first press only brings its part back, and a line that says what a number key did; a short information card that shows each of its parts whole or leaves it out; a shorter Esc page with sentences that say what the motor strip is; a mirror body that turns all the way round and tilts, from its four arrows or a drag, and stands farther back where a turned or tilted body would otherwise reach you; muscles of the left shoulder that stay on the shoulder at far looks; stop-at-contact between the three items; a closed skull, eyes and 111 more muscles from BodyParts3D and Z-Anatomy; a cel-shaded comic look with gloss, lighter ink outlines, inked folds on the motor strip and an HDR glow, with a fix for a white square that covered part of the picture at one exact look; symmetric placement of paired controls; two performance passes. Since 17 November: no start page and no loading page (a picture of the bones, muscles and brain coming together while the files load, drawn by a worker from a copy of the fetched bytes, with the main controls shown for the first five seconds); a quiet first screen (the information cards start off; a tip beside the crosshair names the motor area and its numbered movements, or the muscle or bone; one short prompt; the R key brings the cards); a look that turns half as far again for the same pointer travel. Second upload of 17 November: Space holds a thing and the pointer moves it left, right, up and down across the view, the mirror body included (it lifts off the ground), while the view stays put; a hold or a drag keeps its thing; the mirror body’s head and trunk take all of it and its arms and legs move your own matching limb; both hands close on a grasp; the neck, trunk and left-shoulder muscles light as the look moves the head and arm; the brain drawn as living tissue (pink-grey cortex with lit folds) with strongly coloured motor areas drawn as separate keys, a hover light, a press, and one bright area with a halo, pulse and ring while it is on; a look that reaches 180 degrees to either side, 88 down and 85 up, the eyes turning past the end of the neck’s and chest’s turn; a shorter Esc page. Third upload of 17 November: the lying posture (trunk rounded 68 degrees, neck 22, hips straight), a start look 20 degrees below level and the brain 20 degrees lower, so the first view holds the motor strip, the mirror body and your own chest, arms, legs and feet together; every muscle that crosses a joint (226 of 232) skinned per vertex so that its ends stay on their bones, re-skinned by a third of a degree of joint movement and at most 60,000 vertices a frame; number keys that work with the cards off. Fourth upload of 17 November: a range-of-motion sweep (tools/rom-sweep.mjs) that poses all 108 movements of the body map and six stacks with the game’s own rig and measures muscle ends and joint openings, with its results in section 87. Upload of 18 November: a brain that beats and reacts (it blooms round an area that is switched on and trails and settles when it is carried; fine vessels on its surface), drawn by one shared vertex rule so that aiming is unchanged; a spine that bends at every lumbar and thoracic vertebra with the ribs as a linkage, shoulder girdles that roll forward with the bend, the head carried forward and the eyes lowered in the head; a start look 36 degrees below level with the brain drawn about half as wide; a view from outside that keeps the whole body in the picture. Each of the two packages was built by one helper, tested by an independent checker and fixed by another helper before the author merged it. Second upload of 18 November: a start posture slumped back as on a sofa (the pelvis rolled under by a bend of the low back only, the upper back straight, the neck bent, limbs stretched out with soft elbows and knees); a view taken from 12 cm above the eyes with a field of view of 116 degrees so that the whole torso is in the first picture; chest muscles drawn at about two thirds of the source depth and the belly closed at the midline; the brain beyond and below the feet and larger, with the crosshair starting on the middle of the strip between the legs; a double tap of Space as a quick switch of all four limbs between their underside and overside, the game starting on the underside. Third upload of 18 November: the legs start 7 degrees apart each instead of 12, so the ankles are closer together. Fourth upload of 18 November: the bodies painted with smooth shading, fibre bundles and wet highlights in place of the comic bands; a dark operating theatre out of focus in place of the black void; a leg turn that takes the feet 45 degrees outward and inward in the limb switch; a kneecap that stays on the bending knee; a rule that limits joint angles in combination; small coupled movements at knee, ankle, wrist and hip; a second round of the view (a field of view of 100 degrees from higher and further back, a thinner chest, the left arm along the thigh); and the repair of a fault that had drawn every muscle as one rigid piece in the tenth to twelfth uploads (the skinning had stopped running when the spine was rebuilt). Each package was built by one helper, tested by an independent checker and fixed before the author merged it. Fifth upload of 18 November: bulkier limb muscles, wider far ends of the limbs (bones included), rounded fingers and toes, a thicker neck and muscles that swell as they contract, all as shape steps at load on both bodies; cerebral arteries from BodyParts3D, cerebral veins and sinuses laid by hand from textbook courses, named vessels of the legs and the right arm, and a brain recoloured to be plainly different from muscle; a limb switch that turns the whole arm over. These three packages were merged and published before their independent checks. Sixth upload of 18 November: the eye view through a longer lens from further back (54 degrees, 0.30 m back), which flattens depth and about doubles the limbs in the picture; a new colour code for the motor strip with lines from an area to the part it moves and a blinking, shuddering glow on activity; the layered muscle stack drawn again, smoother shading and cartilage caps; small fixes from an audit of every earlier note, among them that a look only arms a motor area and a click or a number key presses it. These four packages were merged and published before their independent checks. DESIGN-DECISIONS.md sections 20-103 record each change and why. The input-robustness changes published on 11 November (input epochs, deferred input, pointer capture) are included, adapted to the new keys, with their test files.
anatomy_assets: 611 human-anatomy OBJ files. BodyParts3D 4.0 (CC BY 4.0), including the new packets bodyparts3d-head-r1 (cranium and eyes) and missing-muscles-r1 (93 files); Z-Anatomy derivatives (CC BY-SA 4.0): the face muscles and 18 back, belly, neck and foot muscles in missing-muscles-r1. Packet files are unchanged archive members or documented conversions; runtime transforms, lifting, smoothing of finger and toe tips, colouring, comic shading and separated layers are display changes, not physiological validation.

other_project_development: active; priority order: NeuroTranslation, NeuroSurge, Interoceptomics. The Interoceptomics presentation is paused.
known_engineering_gaps: Asked for by the user on 17 and 18 November and NOT in this upload: the mirror body magnified (it is drawn at 0.68 of a true reflection's size and 1.0 m lower); every overlay grouped into a few clear chunks, with the first prompt and the Esc page rewritten for the present controls (they still describe looking as pressing and an older sitting posture); collision effects and one limb pushing another (your own limbs still pass through each other); a limb hidden behind another limb staying visible; a loading picture that builds from the inside out; frame rates (looking around is slower than before); the face; the rest of the audit's list (the left shoulder area's movements, the right elbow with the palm down). Several of these were being built when this version was published.

Muscles and joints, measured by tools/rom-sweep.mjs in the game's own model, now posed as the game draws it (180 poses; the figures below are for the 117 poses of the earlier sweeps, against the start posture). A muscle end more than 8 mm farther from its bone than at the start in 30 of 117 poses (largest 23.2 mm); a joint more than 5 mm farther apart in 8 (largest 8.3 mm); a muscle edge stretched to more than 2.5 times its length in 45; two parts more than 10 mm inside each other in 4 (an estimate). The thirteenth upload had 30 and 8 of 117. The start posture itself against the source pose: 15 of 931 muscle ends more than 8 mm from their bone, largest 22.7 mm in the neck. Known in particular: with the right arm fully raised the armpit is drawn as flat sheets and the top of the shoulder narrows to a point; right subscapularis stands 17 to 23 mm off the shoulder blade; the inward end of the leg turn asks foot, knee and hip for their whole range at once. The sweep does not judge whether a position can be reached from the game's controls. These figures are from the fourteenth upload's build; the sweep was not run again for this upload, which changed the head's carriage, restored the layered stack and re-attached muscles round the hips.

The sixth revision of 18 November (sections 100 to 103) was published before its independent checks. Seen by the author in the start picture: the abdomen is lit in its area's colour from the first frame, on both bodies, without any press; the player's hands and legs cover parts of the motor strip (the legs by the user's wish). Reported by the builders: looking around at 13 frames a second against 22; a dark soft patch where the neck leaves the chest; collar bones and shoulder caps partly cut by the lower edge; the brain's side arrows on the backdrop outside the brain; the left game arm riding up with the look; serratus anterior, latissimus, rhomboid major, trapezius and sternocleidomastoid torn or stretched in the start posture; the shudder too small to judge in still pictures; under simulated protanopia some face keys look like arm keys.

The slumped posture and the view of 18 November. The stomach is a narrow band in the start picture and the legs are seen at a flat angle. The view point is 12 cm above the eyes: the crosshair's line is parallel to the eyes' own, and a full trunk turn moves the view about 12 cm. The field of view of 116 degrees stretches the corners. The brain is not tilted to face the eyes; from outside (E) it is a very large shape under and round the body and hides the pelvis and legs from most sides, and whether the legs clear it everywhere was not measured. The player's legs hide part of the strip's middle (asked for); the crosshair takes the area behind a leg and Shift takes the leg. The left game arm reaches level into the picture instead of lying along the thigh. The trunk's turn and side bend are taken mostly in the low back. Looking up and far round to the right is closed off from 155 degrees. This posture and view were published before their independent check had finished: the trunk movements from the strip, the look extremes, reduced motion and frame rates were not checked on the final build.

Bulk, vessels and the arm turnover (sections 97 to 99) were published before their independent checks. Known: the contraction swell was not seen working in the game; the left game arm has no swell and no vessels; the fingers' new sleeves read as white sausages; the brain's arteries are a strong red that may read as bloody; the veins at the back of the brain can read as rungs; on the overside of the limb switch the right hand swings onto the thigh and can go into the chest; the thigh shows the same muscles on both sides of the switch. The cerebral veins and sinuses were laid by hand from textbook courses and are a typical arrangement, not this brain's own anatomy.

The tenth, eleventh and twelfth uploads drew every muscle as one rigid piece: the per-vertex skinning did not run in the game after the rig grew from 41 to 93 segments (a slot number no longer fitted its 8 bits), and the author's checks, made in software and tests where it ran, did not catch it. It runs in this upload. While things move the game is about a fifth slower than those uploads, which skinned nothing; frame rates were measured on a loaded machine.

The painted look of the bodies: fibres follow each mesh's long line, not always the anatomy (oblique sheets, meshes that hold several muscles); very coarse meshes show flat facets close up; a dotted dark line remains along the tendinous lines of rectus abdominis; bones have no warmer ends and no cartilage tint; arrows and eyes were not restyled; iliacus and psoas, the feet, the face and the mirror body near were not seen close up.

The living brain of 18 November was judged from single frames, edge records and state numbers; nobody has watched the beat, the wobble or the ring in motion. Its vessels are drawn by a rule, not from anatomy. While the brain is carried, the picture and the aim differ by up to about 4 mm for half a second. Labels do not move with the tissue. At low quality levels the brain surface shows ragged dark holes at edge-on views (older defect).

The lying posture and the skinned muscles (this upload) were checked by their author with scripted input in one desktop browser only. The chest still hides most of the belly from the eyes; the look reaches 40 degrees below level instead of 88; the mirror body's head and shoulders stand in front of the leg areas at the lowest part of the strip; the view over the shoulder was not re-framed for the lying body; a muscle bent sharply at a joint is drawn thinner there than a real one. Frame rates in one scripted run on a single processor core shared with the script: looking around 32, bending the trunk 34, the slow limb turn 32, still 60, within that run's noise of the build before.

Holding and moving (this upload): a held thing follows the pointer across the view and the mirror body can be lifted; the mirror body’s limbs move your own. Checked by its author with scripted input in one desktop browser only. The brain is now drawn solid: a limb or the mirror body behind it is hidden by it (move the brain aside, or hold Shift to reach past it), and older notes that speak of seeing through the brain’s glass no longer apply. At far looks to the side the camera turns in the head, so the drawn head on the mirror body stops turning while the view goes on.

The loading picture is a picture only: it draws the atlas files in the atlas's standing posture and plain colours from a copy of the bytes the game fetched, and verifies nothing (the game's loader still checks every file). It needs a worker canvas to keep moving while the page builds the body; without one it is drawn on the page and pauses then. In the author's test browser, which had one processor core, the game was ready after 15 to 17 seconds with the picture and 12 without; on a computer with several cores the difference has not been measured. Checked in one desktop Chromium only.

The view from the eyes is 108 degrees from top to bottom (about 136 across at 16:9). A flat picture that wide stretches what is near its edges: your right arm at the side of a downward look is drawn clearly too large. Seeing everything from the neck down in one level look would need a curved (fisheye) picture, which has not been built.

The first screen now shows far less text. Whether a new player finds the controls from the five-second picture, the tip and the one-line prompt has been checked by the author with scripted input only; nobody else has tried it. The Esc page is still long.

Frame rate in the author's scripted runs at 1920 by 1080 and full picture quality on one desktop computer. One run of this upload: 60 fps sitting still, 59.5-60 looking around, 58.7 in the slow limb turn, 51.1 while holding the mirror body, 51.9 while carrying it (longest frame 50 ms), 57.5 in the view over the shoulder. Seven runs of the fourth upload gave 46-53 holding and 50-54 carrying, so this upload is neither faster nor slower by more than the runs differ. Some frames still take longer than a thirtieth of a second. In the fourth upload the game's own script took about 16.5 ms of each frame while the mirror body was held, which is about all of the 16.7 ms a frame has at 60 fps; that was not measured again for this upload. No performance work went into this upload. More is still to do.

Ease of use and teaching: the changes of the third and fourth uploads (brain above the body, numbered movements, arrow-key steps, the guide’s new order, the teaching sentences; a trunk movement that keeps the view, the line that says how to bring the head back, the “first press brings it back” mark, the short card that leaves out whole parts) were checked by the author with scripted input only. No learner or teacher has tried them, and nothing here shows that the game teaches motor neuroanatomy better than before. The user has since asked for the game to be a lot easier to use and play, more intuitive, and a learning tool for people learning motor neuroanatomy; that work is not in this upload.

Head, trunk and card: after “Tilt head back” and the key that brings the head back, the view ends about 10 degrees above level, below the neck area. While the look is up at the brain, a held forward trunk bend is drawn smaller than the 80 degrees it holds. In a window of 1280 by 720 most short information cards leave out the muscle lines; the R key opens the card that has them.

The motor strip is about 42 % of the view wide at 1920 by 1080; the user asked for 50 %. The brain's bottom arrow sits below the brain's frame edge rather than on it, so that it does not cover the mirror body.

Controls asked for and not built yet: the look swinging a held item round you with the same face toward you; part-way joint positions by brain activation (a movement goes to its end stop); lowering the left arm from the strip (the left shoulder area lists no movements; the arm follows the look and the W A S D keys).

The left shoulder: its muscles now stay on the shoulder at far looks, but at looks far to the left and down the eye is 4 to 7 cm from the shoulder muscle, whose front part shows a ragged border with the upper-arm bone past it, and during the limb turn at such a look a small gap opens between two parts of the muscle.

The mirror body's four arrows stay on the frame round the upright body: a turned or tilted body can reach past that frame, and at a downward look your own left arm can hide the left arrow. Seen from straight above or below, the mirror body fills much of the lower view. The gaps between the turned body and you were measured at the start look and with the limbs at their start only.

The white square at one exact look is gone in pictures taken in headless Chromium on one computer. The shader checks read shader text and cannot show what another graphics card does with it, and the shaders of three.js itself were not gone through for other terms of this kind.
Limbs pass through each other: one limb does not knock another about.
Some motor areas cannot be aimed at until the brain is turned to one side. The count of such areas has not been redone for the 54-area map.
A one-way look lock after a far side look while an item rests against you was reported in the first upload and has not been checked again.

The 11 November input-robustness work (pointer capture boundaries, stale-input cancellation, deferred input queue) is included and covered by scripted tests; it has not been tried in several browsers.
Joint mechanics, whole-body coupling, motor-area registration and timing remain simplified and unvalidated. The body order along the strip is a simplified textbook order.
launcher_scope: Online URL launchers for Windows, macOS and Linux. Formats checked; native Windows/macOS use unverified. Prior Linux installation/launch does not prove execution of this updated target.
publication_status: Experimental preview. Since 12 November 2026 each finished version is uploaded at the user's direct instruction, before the project's independent review. Check the displayed online version before assuming it matches these files.

browser_verification.scope: Author development checks only: scripted mouse and key input in one desktop Chromium, with screenshots, frame-interval counts and profiles, plus one hundred and eighty-nine scripted node tests of the input rules, the picture-quality controller, the number keys, the guide order, the card's settle rule, the arrow-key steps, the words that name an area, the head and trunk rules, the card taking an area in the frame its movement is taken, the skin of the left shoulder, the mirror body's turn and tilt, shader text that must not give a value that is not a number, the loading picture’s file reader and part kinds, the tip beside the crosshair, the limb turn led by wrists and ankles, the collision items, holding and moving with the pointer, the look’s range, the living brain’s rules, the curved spine, the lowered eyes, the view from outside, the picture of the player’s own front, the quick switch of the limbs, the painted look’s rules, the joints (kneecap, combined ranges, leg turn, couplings), the room, the bulk rule and the vessels. Earlier parts were also read and checked by other instances of the same model that wrote them; the changes since the second upload were checked by their author alone. The two packages of 18 November were each tested by a separate instance of the same model that had not written them, with its own scripted pictures, and fixed before merging; that is not an independent review. No independent review yet. Not checked: Firefox, Safari, touch, phones, screen readers, reduced-motion settings in a browser.
